title: Advertising tricks
examples: What is the difference between persuasion and just telling me something?
Can you give me an example of a bandwagon technique?
How do advertisers use famous people in their ads?

explain.say: Today we are learning about advertising tricks. These tricks help ads try to persuade you to buy things.

items: They try to make you feel something.

explain.say: One trick is using celebrities. They make famous people appear in ads. People often trust what famous people say.
Another trick is creating scarcity. This means making you think something is almost gone. It makes you want it right now.
The bandwagon technique is when an ad shows many people using something. It suggests everyone else loves it too.
For a real-life example, consider a new type of shoe. An ad might show many popular kids wearing them. This uses the bandwagon trick.
A common mistake is thinking all ads are always honest. Remember that advertisers are trying to persuade you. Always think critically about what you see.

items: Ads are persuasive, not always factual.
Look for evidence beyond the ad.
Question the claims made to you.

faq.q: What is the difference between persuasion and just telling me something?
faq.a: Telling you something is just stating a fact. Persuasion tries to change your feelings or actions about that fact.
asks: How is it different from informing?

faq.q: Can a celebrity endorsement be fake?
faq.a: Yes, sometimes the connection is not genuine. The celebrity might just be paid to look good with the product.
asks: Do celebrities always like the products they advertise?
Is it always believable when a star promotes something?

faq.q: What does scarcity mean in advertising?
faq.a: It means making you feel like the product is running out quickly. This pressure makes you buy it without thinking much.
asks: Why do ads say 'limited time only'?
Is running out of stock a real reason to buy?

faq.q: Is the bandwagon technique always manipulative?
faq.a: It can be, because it plays on your desire to fit in. It suggests that if others like it, you should too.
asks: Is it okay to use the bandwagon technique?

faq.q: Are these tricks used in all types of advertising?
faq.a: These techniques are very common across many media types. You will see them in TV, print, and online ads.
asks: Do ads on social media use these tricks?
Where can I find these advertising techniques?

facts: Persuasion aims to influence belief or action.
Celebrity endorsements rely on the audience's trust in the person.
Scarcity tactics create a sense of urgency to purchase.
The bandwagon technique suggests widespread acceptance.

quiz.say: An ad shows a product with a countdown timer ticking down to zero. Which trick is this?
quiz.why: The timer creates urgency, making you think you must buy it before it is too late.

wrong.0: Bandwagon shows many people using it, not just a timer.
wrong.1: A celebrity would usually be pictured, not just a timer.
wrong.2: Persuasion is too general; scarcity is the specific trick used here.

quiz.say: A famous movie star appears in an ad for toothpaste. What technique is the ad primarily using?
quiz.why: The star's fame is used to build trust and positive feelings toward the product.

wrong.0: Bandwagon requires showing many different people using it.
wrong.1: While it is persuasive, 'Celebrity' names the specific technique used.
wrong.3: There is no mention of limited stock or time running out.

quiz.say: An ad shows hundreds of people happily using a new brand of cereal. What trick is this?
quiz.why: Showing many people using it suggests that the product is popular and safe to buy.

wrong.0: No famous person is featured in this advertisement.
wrong.1: Bandwagon is the specific technique; persuasion is the general goal.
wrong.3: Scarcity relates to how much is left, not how many people use it.
